citations.text: Section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 lists the deductions from salary income and replaces section 16 of the 1961 Act. The standard deduction is ₹75,000 or the amount of salary, whichever is less, where income-tax is computed under the new regime of section 202(1), and ₹50,000 or the salary, whichever is less, in any other case (the old regime). The amounts are unchanged from FY 2025-26. It is available to salaried employees and pensioners automatically, with no proof needed. Self-employed people and freelancers with only business or professional income do not get it.

Is 80C still available in the new Income.answer: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. [IT-MAP-80C] Yes, the 80C deduction still exists from Tax Year 2026-27, only under a new number: section 123 allows up to ₹1,50,000 for the payments listed in Schedule XV (PF, PPF, life insurance, ELSS, tuition fees, home-loan principal and so on). [IT-MAP-80C] Under section 202(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, total income in the new regime is computed without most exemptions in Schedule III (such as house rent allowance and leave travel concession) and without the deductions in Chapter VIII, except a few carved out: section 124(1) and 124(2) (pension scheme contributions, including the employer's NPS contribution, the old section 80CCD(2), up to 14% of salary), section 125(2) (Agniveer Corpus Fund) and section 146. [IT-NEW-DEDUCTIONS-TY2627]

citations.text: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Yes, the 80C deduction still exists from Tax Year 2026-27, only under a new number: section 123 allows up to ₹1,50,000 for the payments listed in Schedule XV (PF, PPF, life insurance, ELSS, tuition fees, home-loan principal and so on). The pension deductions of sections 80CCC and 80CCD of the 1961 Act — including 80CCD(1B) self NPS and 80CCD(2) employer NPS — correspond to section 124 of the 2025 Act. Chapter VI-A of the 1961 Act (sections 80A to 80U) as a whole becomes Chapter VIII of the 2025 Act, roughly sections 123 to 154. For FY 2025-26 returns filed in 2026, you still quote section 80C.

So the old 80C (now section 123), 80D (now 126), 80TTA/80TTB (now 153), HRA and self-occupied home-loan interest cannot be claimed. Loss from house property cannot be set off against other heads. citations.source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
citations.text: Section 202(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (which replaces section 115BAC of the 1961 Act) sets the default new-regime rates for individuals, HUFs, AOPs, BOIs and artificial juridical persons from Tax Year 2026-27: total income up to ₹4,00,000 – nil; ₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 – 5%; ₹8,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 – 10%; ₹12,00,001 to ₹16,00,000 – 15%; ₹16,00,001 to ₹20,00,000 – 20%; ₹20,00,001 to ₹24,00,000 – 25%; above ₹24,00,000 – 30%. The rates are the same as for FY 2025-26; Budget 2026 did not change the slabs. Unlike the 1961 Act, the slabs are written into the Act itself. The same rates apply to senior and super-senior citizens. A 4% health and education cess is added on tax plus surcharge.

citations.title: Old tax regime slabs for individuals below 60 years
citations.source_title: Old tax regime — slab rates, rebate and deductions (Income-tax Act, 1961 Finance Acts; Finance Act 2026 First Schedule for Tax Year 2026-27)
citations.text: Under the old (optional) tax regime, an individual below 60 years pays: income up to ₹2,50,000 – nil; ₹2,50,001 to ₹5,00,000 – 5%; ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 – 20%; above ₹10,00,000 – 30%. Cumulative tax is ₹12,500 at ₹5 lakh and ₹1,12,500 at ₹10 lakh, plus 4% cess. These rates have not changed for many years: they applied for FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and the Finance Act, 2026 keeps the same basic exemption of ₹2,50,000 for Tax Year 2026-27 for people who opt out of section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The old regime allows deductions such as 80C, 80D, HRA and home-loan interest, and a standard deduction of ₹50,000.

citations.title: Section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — presumptive taxation from Tax Year 2026-27
citations.source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
citations.text: From Tax Year 2026-27, sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE of the 1961 Act are consolidated into a single section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in a table format. The core rules carry over: eligible professionals declare 50% of gross receipts as profit (receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh if cash receipts are within 5%); eligible small businesses declare 8% of turnover, or 6% of digital/banking receipts (turnover up to ₹2 crore, or ₹3 crore if cash is within 5%); and goods-carriage owners with up to ten vehicles use per-vehicle income. Commentators note some tightening, such as stricter disqualification for minor commission income and a full bar on setting off losses against presumptive income. The tax-audit provision (old section 44AB) corresponds to section 63.

citations.title: GST registration for freelancers, consultants and content creators
citations.source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 2(6), 22, 24, 25; CGST Rules 8, 9, 14A; Notification 10/2019-CT; Notification 10/2017-IT; PIB release on 56th GST Council (trade facilitation)
citations.text: Freelancers, consultants, designers, developers, tutors and content creators supply services, so the services threshold applies: registration is required once aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds Rs 20 lakh (Rs 10 lakh in Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura). Billing clients in other states does not by itself force registration for service providers below this limit, because Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax exempts inter-state service suppliers up to the threshold. Most professional services, such as consulting, software, design and advertising, are taxed at 18%. Income from foreign clients is an export of services, which is zero-rated: once registered, the freelancer can export without paying IGST by filing a Letter of Undertaking (LUT, Form GST RFD-11), but export receipts still count in aggregate turnover. Detailed export and refund questions should be taken to a CA.

citations.source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
citations.text: Up to 21 September 2025, air-conditioners (HSN 8415) and dishwashing machines (HSN 8422) were taxed at 28% GST. Television sets and monitors larger than 32 inches were also at 28%, while TVs and monitors up to 32 inches were at 18%. Refrigerators and washing machines were not in the 28% slab during this period: they had already been cut from 28% to 18% from 27 July 2018. So an AC bought in August 2025 carried 28% GST, a 43-inch LED TV 28%, and a refrigerator or washing machine 18%. These are the old, pre-GST 2.0 rates and apply to sales up to 21 September 2025.

citations.title: Section 156 — rebate up to ₹60,000 if total income is up to ₹12 lakh (Tax Year 2026-27)
citations.source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
citations.text: Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces section 87A of the 1961 Act. Under section 156(2), a resident individual taxed under the new regime of section 202(1) gets a rebate equal to 100% of tax or ₹60,000, whichever is less, if total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000. So there is effectively no tax up to ₹12 lakh of taxable income (₹12.75 lakh of salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction). For income above ₹12 lakh, marginal relief applies: the tax payable cannot exceed the amount by which total income exceeds ₹12,00,000. Section 156(1) keeps the old-regime rebate of up to ₹12,500 for total income up to ₹5,00,000. Only resident individuals qualify; HUFs, firms and non-residents do not.
